summary: Defines techniques for representing two types of information mapping in the OSI Directory, tables and subtrees. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 2293.

plainLanguage.summary: Ways to store lookup lists inside a giant directory so programs can use them.

questions: how to store tables in x.500
what are subtrees in the x.500 directory
why use tables instead of subtrees
subtitle: Techniques for storing lookup tables and hierarchies in the OSI Directory.

tldr.problem: The X.500 Directory needs ways to represent key-value mappings (tables) and information organized in hierarchies when objects lack natural global names or when information belongs in a separate context.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1837 defines two approaches: tables as single-level subtrees with text or distinguished-name keys, and subtrees as hierarchies with distinguished names relative to a private root.
tldr.outcome: This experimental approach was later superseded by RFC 2293, which refined these techniques for use in X.500 directories and message handling systems.

today: RFC 1837 is an Experimental protocol and has been obsoleted by RFC 2293. For modern applications, RFC 2293 provides refined techniques for representing tables and subtrees in the X.500 Directory.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: RFC 1837 defines techniques for representing two types of information mapping in the OSI Directory (X.500). The first maps keys to values, like a lookup table. The second associates values with distinguished names without requiring the object owner to define them. These techniques were developed to support Message Handling System (MHS) use of the Directory.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC shows two ways to store information lookups inside the X.500 Directory: one for simple key-value lists and one for information tied to existing directory objects.

sections.title: Flat Tables
sections.content:
A table is represented as a single-level subtree rooted at an entry of class Table. The table contains key-to-value mappings where keys cannot be represented as global names for four reasons: the object has no natural global name, it only makes sense as a key in this context, it has a global name but the parameters cannot go in the global entry, or grouping the information together improves replication performance.

Two subclasses are defined. TextTableEntry holds entries with text keys and optional text values. DistinguishedNameTableEntry associates information with globally defined objects using distinguished names as keys. The example in the RFC shows mapping private domain nicknames (like 'euclid' to 'bloomsbury.ac.uk') in a table under an MTA's directory entry.
sections.plainLanguage: A table entry is like a card in a catalog: it has a key (the label) and a value (the information). The RFC defines how to store these cards inside the directory so programs can look them up.

sections.title: Subtrees
sections.content:
A subtree is similar to a table but uses a hierarchy of distinguished names relative to the subtree's root. The subtree effectively starts a private root and has distinguished names relative to it. This approach is typically used to associate local information with global objects. Unlike tables, no specific object classes are defined for subtree entries; information is defined using the same structure as for the global object.

The subtree object class defines only the root with a common name and optional manager. For example, University College London might define a private subtree containing UCL-specific information about other directory objects, such as details about Inria stored under a hierarchy rooted at the subtree entry.
sections.plainLanguage: A subtree is like a private filing cabinet beside the main directory. You can organize information inside it using the same naming structure as the main directory, but it is just for your organization.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content: The RFC includes no discussion of security considerations, stating only that security issues are not addressed in the memo. This is an Experimental protocol, and implementers should consult RFC 2293 and related specifications for guidance on secure use of tables and subtrees in operational Directory deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not discuss how to keep the tables and subtrees safe from unauthorized access. Implementers need to think about security separately.
